title: A predictive theory of pelagic size structure and trophic transfer

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a theory that predicts how biomass is distributed among body sizes in open-water marine food webs, and how biological production passes from phytoplankton toward larger consumers, including fish. Starting from temperature, nutrients, the phytoplankton size spectrum and any necessary biological state, it would predict how the community’s biomass spectrum steepens or flattens as environmental conditions change. Its defining capability would be successful prediction in marine biomes and environmental conditions withheld from fitting.

Body size is a major organizing trait because it influences feeding and other ecological processes. A biomass size spectrum describes how standing biomass is distributed across organism sizes; its slope summarizes how that distribution changes toward larger organisms. However, standing biomass and production are different quantities. A theory that predicts the spectrum would still need to predict or otherwise constrain production and turnover to establish how efficiently new production reaches consumers.

The target is an environmental prediction of aggregate food-web organization, rather than simply a relationship fitted to observed spectra. Size supplies a useful organizing variable, but its sufficiency cannot be assumed: food quality, community composition, predator–prey mass ratios and turnover can alter the relationships between environmental conditions, biomass and production.

significance.text: If independently validated, this theory would provide a fundamental link between environmental forcing and the organization of pelagic food webs. It could turn changes in temperature, nutrients and the phytoplankton community into quantitative predictions of aggregate consumer biomass and production. That would move beyond describing a present-day spectrum or tuning a model to reproduce it, toward explaining and anticipating food-web responses across environments.

A central consequence would be better prediction of trophic amplification: a change near the food-web base can correspond to a larger proportional change in the biomass supported at higher levels. Atkinson and colleagues document substantial disagreement among models about the magnitude and mechanisms of that amplification. A theory that resolved those mechanisms and passed independent tests would make the consequences of environmental change more interpretable and constrain a major source of uncertainty in projections.

Conditional downstream uses include improved estimates of the biological production available to fish and better constraints on ecosystem responses to climate change. These would not automatically yield species-specific stock forecasts or fisheries yields. Biomass spectra alone do not determine production, and organisms of similar size can differ ecologically and biochemically. Likewise, connections between size structure and the biological carbon pump would not by themselves establish particle-scale carbon-export predictions. The breakthrough would therefore be a general predictive framework for aggregate pelagic organization, with a demonstrated domain of applicability, rather than a complete law of every food-web outcome.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability sought here is a predictive closure: a sufficiently complete set of relationships connecting environmental and biological state to biomass size structure and production transfer without refitting the answer separately for each environment. The supplied 2024 paper establishes model disagreement and difficult validation as motivations for this goal. It does not establish that every existing approach fails to generalize, or that no such closure exists as of 1 November 2026.

A scientific barrier is identifying which mechanisms determine the spectrum and its response. Changes in the phytoplankton baseline can propagate through consumers, while temperature may affect both the food-web base and consumers directly. Food quality, composition and predator–prey size relationships can change the outcome even when aggregate size structure looks similar. A useful closure must determine when size and environmental measurements are sufficient and when additional biological variables are necessary.

A separate barrier is connecting biomass to rates. Similar standing biomasses can have different turnover and production, so predicting a biomass slope cannot alone establish transfer efficiency or fish production. The broader innovation requires dynamics that connect biomass with production and independent observations capable of testing those dynamics.

Validation also faces problems of scale and extrapolation. An empirical relationship across locations may not describe change through time at one location, and broad spatial or temporal averages may have limited local predictive power. Assuming a linear spectrum or substituting spatial differences for temporal responses can make a projection tractable without establishing that the underlying relationships remain valid under environmental change. Resolving these issues requires observations and modelling matched to the scales and organism sizes being predicted.

current_state.text: In Nature Communications on 9 January 2024, Atkinson, Rossberg, Gaedke, Sprules, Heneghan, Batziakas, Grigoratou, Fileman, Schmidt and Frangoulis compiled pelagic size spectra and examined an empirical relationship between spectrum slope and chlorophyll. Their synthesis combines marine and freshwater observations, which matters when interpreting it as evidence for a specifically marine predictive theory. The paper documents existing size-based modelling approaches and disagreement over trophic-amplification mechanisms; the supplied review does not establish the broader state of trait-based modelling through separately inspected model studies.

The paper’s numerical illustration concerns the North Atlantic region 30–60°N, 70°W–10°E. Using outputs from two Earth system models under SSP5-8.5, coupled to the empirical slope–chlorophyll relationship, it associates a 16% decline in phytoplankton biomass with a 38% decline in supportable fish biomass between 1990–1999 and 2090–2099. This is a conditional extrapolation, not an observed decline in fish stocks or a demonstrated forecast of actual future stocks. It assumes spectrum linearity and uses spatial relationships to infer temporal change.

The analysis associates spectrum slopes and amplification mainly with conditions at the phytoplankton baseline. It finds no strong independent direct thermal effect on consumers in that analysis, while allowing that such effects may be obscured. This supports a baseline-centered interpretation of the reported relationship without ruling out consumer temperature effects or settling the mechanisms across all environments. The authors also distinguish biomass attenuation through food webs from changes in production, limiting what their spectra alone demonstrate about production transfer and fisheries yields.

The evidence available here supports these dated findings, but does not provide a field-wide assessment through 1 November 2026: no bounded freshness-search entries were supplied. The supplied review relied on retained full main-article text, with figure images and linked supplements treated separately. The source index also lists supplementary files, including one whose text extraction was truncated; the review does not establish complete examination of those materials. These limits constrain claims about subsequent progress and supplementary detail, without invalidating the documented 2024 findings.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: fit the theory without data from selected marine basins or biomes, then predict their biomass-spectrum slopes and consumer-biomass responses from independently measured environmental and biological inputs. Compare predictive skill with an empirical polynomial regression on chlorophyll and other explicitly specified baselines. A global compilation of observed slopes would provide valuable evidence, but would not by itself demonstrate this withheld-environment capability.
completion_criteria.label: Predict withheld-biome biomass-spectrum slopes and consumer-biomass responses against baselines

completion_criteria.text: Proposed temporal test: predict the direction and magnitude of change during a documented phytoplankton shift in an environment excluded from temporal calibration. Specify the spatial and temporal averaging, consumer size range, forecast interval, uncertainty treatment and skill metrics before evaluating the predictions. Spatial generalization and temporal response should both be tested because success at one does not establish the other.
completion_criteria.label: Predict phytoplankton-shift change direction and magnitude outside temporal calibration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed production test: independently evaluate production or turnover predictions alongside biomass predictions. Demonstrate that the theory can account for the production reaching defined consumer size classes, including a stated fish size range, with uncertainty consistent with the observations. This additional test is necessary to demonstrate the trophic-transfer component of the innovation rather than only its biomass-structure component.
completion_criteria.label: Independently validate production reaching consumer sizes, including stated fish sizes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary requirements: make the model, parameter-estimation procedure, evaluation data and uncertainty calculations available so independent groups can repeat the tests. Report where predictions succeed or fail across contrasting conditions, and distinguish aggregate biomass or production from species-specific stock and yield forecasts. These are proposed evidentiary requirements, not established standards; finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within specified boundaries, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Enable independent test reproduction and report predictive successes, failures, and boundaries

related_concepts.text: OCE-03, “A predictive closure of the biological carbon pump,” is the closest related target. The supplied paper connects organism size and ecological differences to carbon-pump processes, providing a mechanistic overlap with OCE-09. The distinction is the quantity to be predicted: OCE-09 targets pelagic biomass organization and production transfer, whereas OCE-03’s supplied title identifies biological carbon-pump closure. Neither success automatically establishes the other, and the supplied material does not establish that bulk tracers alone would be sufficient for OCE-03.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-01, “A closed theory of oceanic turbulent transport,” and OCE-07, “The stability class of the global overturning circulation,” concern physical processes that could shape the environmental forcing supplied to a pelagic theory. Their targets remain distinct from predicting food-web responses to that forcing. OCE-02, “Synoptic sensing of the ocean interior,” could complement OCE-09 by improving environmental observations, but a sensing capability would not itself supply a biological closure.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-04, “Persistent mobile operations at full ocean depth,” and OCE-10, “Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing,” concern operational capabilities that could support ocean observations. OCE-05, “Closure of ocean–crust fluid and biogeochemical exchange,” OCE-06, “A verified law of ice-shelf basal melting,” and OCE-08, “Continuous centimeter-level geodesy of the seismogenic seafloor,” have different primary targets from pelagic size structure. The supplied roster establishes no more specific dependency between these entries and OCE-09; they remain separate innovations.

unresolved_issues: Whether a theory already meets some or all of the proposed spatial, temporal and production-transfer tests as of 1 November 2026 remains unresolved; no freshness-search record was supplied.
The minimum biological state needed in addition to temperature, nutrients and phytoplankton size structure remains unspecified.
The degree to which the mixed marine–freshwater empirical relationship transfers across marine biomes and through temporal environmental changes remains to be demonstrated.
The relative contributions of phytoplankton-baseline changes and direct consumer thermal effects remain uncertain beyond the supplied analysis.
Numerical acceptance thresholds, evaluation scales, consumer size ranges and uncertainty criteria for a convincing demonstration have not been selected.
The supplied review does not establish complete examination of figure images or supplementary materials; one indexed supplementary text extraction was truncated.
OCE-03’s detailed scope and any claim about the sufficiency of bulk tracers require evidence beyond its supplied title and the documented mechanistic overlap.

brief.title: Predicting how ocean food webs support larger animals
possible: Scientists could predict how warming seas and changing nutrients alter the amount of life supported at different body sizes, from tiny organisms to fish. The same theory would work in ocean environments it had never been fitted to.
It would also predict how much new living material passes from phytoplankton, the microscopic organisms that photosynthesize, to larger animals through feeding.
why: Changes at the bottom of an ocean food web can produce larger proportional changes higher up. Explaining this amplification would help scientists anticipate how environmental change affects the food available to fish.

A successful theory would connect ocean conditions to the organization and productivity of whole food webs. It would reduce uncertainty in projections of how marine ecosystems respond to climate change.

sources.showed: Their synthesis linked lower phytoplankton abundance to a sharper decline in biomass, the amount of living material, toward larger body sizes. It combined marine and freshwater observations.
sources.quote: Our global compilation of pelagic size spectrum slopes supports trophic amplification empirically, independently from model simulations.
sources.cited_for: The study supports the case that changes at the food-web base can amplify toward larger animals.
sources.not_established: The relationship does not establish predictions in unfamiliar marine environments or how much new production reaches fish.

sources.showed: Across five ocean regions, more productive ecosystems had relatively more large plankton, organisms that drift in water. Size patterns had only a weak relationship with the fraction of production carried downward by sinking particles.
sources.quote:
While organic carbon export co‐varied with NBSS slope, we found only weak evidence that export
efficiency is related to plankton community size spectra.
sources.cited_for: The measurements connect plankton size patterns with productivity and test their relationship with sinking carbon.
sources.not_established: These observed relationships do not demonstrate predictions of food-web responses or production reaching fish.

sources.showed: They released a global database of marine particle size distributions measured with imaging devices.
sources.cited_for: The database provides observations for testing predictions of ocean size structure.
sources.not_established: A database of observed size patterns does not itself demonstrate successful predictions in unfamiliar environments.

shown: Atkinson and colleagues found broad patterns linking the food-web base to the relative biomass of small and large organisms. Their analysis associated amplification mainly with conditions shaping phytoplankton, while leaving direct temperature effects on consumers unresolved.

Stukel and colleagues paired marine plankton size measurements with productivity and sinking-carbon measurements. These studies establish relationships to explain and test; they do not demonstrate a theory that predicts both biomass and production across unfamiliar ocean conditions.
missing: The target requires successful predictions in unfamiliar marine environments without fitting the theory again for each place.
Predictions must connect the biomass present with how quickly organisms grow and are replaced, establishing production reaching larger animals.
Tests must establish whether relationships across places also predict changes through time.

milestones.label: Accurate size patterns and animal biomass in unfamiliar oceans
milestones.explanation: A theory would have to predict how biomass changes with body size and how consumer biomass responds in marine regions excluded from fitting, against simpler statistical baselines. This would establish prediction across environments.

milestones.label: Accurate responses to a change in phytoplankton
milestones.explanation: A test would have to predict the direction and size of changes during a phytoplankton shift excluded from temporal fitting, using evaluation rules set beforehand. This would establish prediction through time.

milestones.label: Accurate production reaching larger animals, including fish
milestones.explanation: Independent measurements would have to confirm predicted production or replacement rates alongside biomass, including a defined fish size range. This would establish how much new living material reaches larger animals.

milestones.label: Independent repeat tests and clear limits
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to repeat tests using shared models, fitting methods, data and uncertainty calculations, with successes and failures reported. This would establish where aggregate predictions work and their limits.

uncertain: It remains unclear which biological information is needed beyond temperature, nutrients and phytoplankton size patterns.
Food quality, species composition and direct temperature effects on consumers may alter the relationships.
The accuracy, averaging scales and consumer size ranges needed for a convincing demonstration remain undecided.

page.title: Predictive theory of pelagic size spectra and trophic transfer
page.definition: A theory predicts biomass by body size in open-water marine food webs and the fraction of production by phytoplankton, microscopic photosynthetic organisms, reaching larger consumers, including fish. Its predictions retain skill in marine regions and periods excluded from calibration, without local refitting.

goal.need: A global size-based model placed marine consumer biomass within a 90% uncertainty interval of 0.3–26.1 billion tonnes for organisms weighing 1 g–1000 kg. Uncertainty came chiefly from trophic transfer efficiency and predator–prey mass ratios. Biomass spectra alone do not establish production, so predicting transfer to consumers also requires rates.

statements.body: Marine Ecosystems Research Programme, funded by NERC and Defra
statements.quote: a whole-system perspective is now required linking an understanding of the dynamics of marine ecological communities into the currency of ecosystem services
statements.context: The programme's broader goal was to integrate marine ecosystem observations and models; it did not specify a completion test for this joint predictive theory.

statements.body: Fisheries and Marine Ecosystem Model Intercomparison Project (FishMIP)
statements.quote: models that can robustly detect past and project future ecosystem changes and risks to the services that they provide to people.
statements.context: FishMIP 2.0 sets a broader goal for marine ecosystem models and introduces historical evaluation before climate-impact projections.

completion.title: Independent validation confirms predictions of marine size spectra and production outside calibration.
completion.criterion: An independent group validates one frozen theory against measured living-biomass size spectra and production reaching consumer size classes, including fish, in marine regions and periods excluded from calibration. Without local refitting, modelling efficiency (MEF) exceeds 0 separately for spectrum slopes, biomass by size and consumer production in each validation dataset: MEF = 1 − Σ(P−O)²/Σ(O−mean(O))², where P denotes predictions and O observations. Size ranges and averaging scales are fixed before evaluation; production is measured independently of predicted biomass. Error and correlation diagnostics accompany MEF.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body located specifies the combined capability, validation domain and acceptance test.
completion.basis: Searches of FishMIP/ISIMIP protocols, NERC/Defra MERP, SCOR, ICES and marine-model validation literature found no joint acceptance test for size spectra and production outside calibration. This fallback combines published independent-verification practice and the MEF > 0 benchmark. FishMIP distinguishes state, process and system assessment; its 2025 application evaluated catches. Independent validation of both stocks and rates supplies the narrowest joint test.

milestones.title: A plankton model reproduces grazing and production responses across three temperatures.
milestones.criterion: Reproduce the observed directions of consumer responses in the published marine microcosm comparison: six nutrient treatments, three temperatures (means 13.7, 19.5 and 23.4 °C), and four consumer treatments (Euplotes vannus, Brachionus plicatilis, both, or neither). Warming increased grazing and production; poorer algal food increased grazing but reduced growth and final biovolume. Moorthi et al., published on 19 May 2016, reported qualitative model agreement. This supports component mechanisms; it does not validate a complete biomass spectrum.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback using Moorthi et al.'s published experimental comparison; no numerical laboratory acceptance threshold was found.

milestones.title: Marine plankton spectrum slopes correlate positively with primary production at p < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: Test the published hypothesis that higher net primary production accompanies a less negative normalized biomass size-spectrum slope, using Spearman rank correlation with p < 0.05. Normalization divides biomass in a size bin by its width. Stukel et al. tested carbon-based spectra from five ocean regions and reported ρ = 0.36, p < 10⁻³ in 2024. This establishes an environmental association, rather than prediction in withheld regions or measurement of consumer production.
milestones.set_by: Stukel et al. (2024), published hypothesis and statistical protocol, Sections 1 and 2.3 and Figure 3; the five-region scope is specific to this study.

milestones.title: A pelagic biomass-spectrum model beats the observed-mean baseline on independent observations.
milestones.criterion: For marine living-biomass spectra in data excluded from parameter estimation, obtain MEF > 0: squared prediction error is smaller than the error from predicting the observed mean. PSSdb, released on 26 June 2024, supplies particle spectra from three sensors, including detritus. A study published on 29 November 2025 compared seven Earth system models with PSSdb: median biovolume-spectrum slopes ranged from −1.66 to −1.07 versus −1.05 observed. Those median comparisons do not establish this independent living-biomass skill test.
milestones.set_by: Marine-model skill convention documented by Stow et al. (2009) and applied by Olsen et al. (2016). MEF > 0 is a general predictive-skill benchmark, not a spectrum-specific certification.
milestones.threshold_quote: A value of zero indicates that the model predicts individual observations no better than the average of the observations.

milestones.title: One theory predicts marine size spectra and consumer production outside calibration with MEF > 0.
milestones.criterion: One frozen theory achieves MEF > 0 separately for spectrum slopes, biomass by size and independently measured consumer production, including fish, in withheld marine regions and time intervals, without local refitting. This is the joint state-and-rate demonstration before independent validation. FishMIP's 2025 assessment tested catches from two models and called for production and trophic-transfer outputs; it did not report this joint result.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback combining FishMIP's state, process and system assessment categories with the published MEF benchmark; no joint milestone threshold was located.

not_found: No published acceptance test was located for joint prediction of marine biomass size spectra and production transfer outside calibration.
No independently validated result meeting the joint completion criterion was located in the searched literature.
Microcosm replicate counts and the observation count underlying Stukel et al.'s correlation could not be verified from the accessible material.
The full text of the 2026 paper Temperature, trophic state, and carrying capacity govern pelagic size spectra in the Atlantic Ocean could not be opened; its author-project abstract was accessible.

results.finding: Across 23 marine ecosystems, normalized biomass-spectrum slopes were positively related to chlorophyll a.
results.detail: Chlorophyll a is a proxy for phytoplankton biomass, not a measurement of primary production. The reported analysis used regression rather than the specified Spearman correlation.
results.quote:
This underlying difference between lakes and the sea was not driving the relationships because when both systems were considered separately the positive relationships with Chl
a
and lack of relationship with temperature were preserved

results.finding: Across five ocean regions, net primary production and whole-community biomass-spectrum slope had Spearman ρ = 0.36.
results.detail: The correlation was positive and significant (p < 0.001). This is an environmental association, not a test of prediction in withheld regions.

results.finding: Marine plankton model qualitatively reproduced grazing and production responses in 288 microcosm flasks.
results.detail: The experiment combined six nutrient treatments, three temperatures and four consumer treatments. Model parameters were fitted to the experimental data; agreement was qualitative, with exceptions for grazing responses. This does not validate a complete biomass spectrum.
results.quote: Overall, model predictions reflected experimental patterns well: consumer grazing rates and production increased with temperature, as could be expected based on MTE.

results.finding: In a 288-flask marine microcosm experiment, a model reproduced the decline in consumer growth and final biovolume with increasing algal C : N.
results.detail: The model was fitted to the experimental data. The study did not report size-spectrum predictions, fish production, withheld marine regions or periods, or MEF.
results.quote: Our model predicted a decrease in consumer growth rates and final consumer biovolume with increasing C : N ratios, which could also be observed in our experiment.

results.finding: Mesoplankton size-spectrum models: 3,068 UVP profiles and 2,411 scans overall; reported R² was 0.79 for crustaceans.
results.detail: The reported R² describes model goodness of fit. The text does not establish that observations were excluded from parameter estimation or report MEF against the observed-mean baseline.
results.quote:
Using environmental explanatory variables, our models reached high R
2
(0.93, 0.88, and 0.79 respectively), providing robust predictions of mesoplankton size structure related to elemental cycling and ecosystem services.
